model_card.name: Kolaboro risk patterns
model_card.purpose: Show which tracked projects look unusual on public warning signs compared with all other tracked projects, and why. It ranks; it does not predict.
model_card.not_for: It is not a fraud predictor and not a verdict. No project in our data has a confirmed outcome (fraud, collapse or delivery), so nothing could be trained or tested against outcomes.

features.label: Months the completion date has moved
Permit claim contradicted by a register or document
Checks contradicted by an independent source
Public problems reported (disputes, complaints, regulator action)
Not on the official approval register checked
Sold as under construction, no visible change on satellite

features_not_available.why: Share of the price due before construction starts. Payment plans are read only from documents buyers upload, not for every tracked project, so it is not in the model yet.
Advertised price versus official sales. Public data holds only a price band per project, too coarse for a per-project feature (see /prices/).

method: Each feature is turned into a robust z-score against all 891 tracked projects. Yes/no signs: (1 - p) / sqrt(p (1 - p)) when present, where p is the share of projects showing it, so a rare sign weighs more than a common one. Numbers: (x - median) / (1.4826 x MAD). Numbers that most projects do not have at all (overdue months, contradicted checks, public problems): the same rarity term for having any, plus a robust z of the size among the projects that have it (0 to 4). Every contribution is capped at 8, and only the risky direction counts: absence of a sign adds nothing.

The score is the sum of these z-scores, so every point of it is traceable to one feature. Projects at or above the 95th percentile of the score are labelled "unusual", at or above the 75th "somewhat unusual".

Cross-check: an isolation forest (500 trees, random_state 7, scikit-learn) on the raw features, with no labels. Its ranking is published next to ours; where both put a project in the top 5%%, the pattern is not an artefact of our weighting.
limits: Features come from what developers publish and what we could check; a project that publishes less can look calmer than it is.
Common signs (no deposit protection stated, no permit claimed) weigh little because most projects show them; that is a property of the peer group, not a judgement that they are safe.
Peers are all tracked projects in every market, so market norms (for example yields in Bali) affect scores.
Features overlap with the public disclosure score; this view adds rarity weighting and the cross-check, not new facts.
Scores change when the dataset changes; each version is tied to the dataset SHA-256 above.

keys.r: percentile of score among all projects
keys.c: [feature, z contribution, raw value] for every feature that contributes
